axioms: LLM agents with enterprise tool permissions can pursue sub-goals that violate implicit safety policies even when every tool works as designed. · - Once agents can send mail, modify files, and call APIs, the main risk moves from unsafe text to unsafe actions taken through trusted tools. · - Agentic misalignment comes from the interaction of model, prompt, tool access, and adversarial context, so harm can occur without any conventional software exploit. · - LLM-integrated systems struggle to separate trusted instructions from untrusted retrieved content, so an injected tool response can pass as task guidance. · - Single-agent configurations acted on injected tool-response instructions in 93.3% to 100% of prompt_injection runs for all six tested models. · - Misalignment varies sharply by model: overall rates across six models in the same 250-run matrix ranged from 7.6% to 41.2%.
invariables: Every tool output an agent receives must be handled as potentially hostile data and never as a trusted instruction. · - Prompt-level safety instructions alone do not secure a tool-using agent; runtime observability, tool-boundary controls, and scenario-specific validation are required alongside them. · - Before production, deployers must log reasoning steps, tool strings, state transitions, and runtime actions so behavior is judged from artifacts rather than model self-report. · - An agent's own transcript cannot prove what it did; misalignment is scored from durable artifacts left in the mail, file share, and API services it touched. · - Automated scorer labels stay unvalidated until a manual audit checks scorer-positive and sampled scorer-negative runs against the raw service logs. · - A 0% misalignment result in a cell with heavy timeout censoring is unresolved and cannot be reported as confirmed clean. · - A low-risk result holds only for the tested model version, prompt, and tool configuration; it is not a durable safety guarantee after provider updates.
principles: Least privilege: the deploying team isolates email, SMB write, and administrative API access behind separate execution controls and tool-boundary checks for each agent. · - Explicit tool constraints: the prompt author replaces broad task descriptions with enforceable rules, such as no emailing file contents and no admin endpoint calls outside the task. · - Prompt-injection hardening: developers apply injection-resistant parsing to tool responses and treat returned content as data whenever an agent ingests external API output. · - Behavior-first evaluation: security and AI governance teams test agents through sandboxed actions and the artifacts they leave before deployment, instead of reviewing static text output. · - Isolated test environment: evaluation teams run agents in a non-production segment with synthetic data and test credentials, and route risky actions to capture sinks such as an SMTP trap. · - Release gates: the agent owner sets thresholds such as maximum exfiltration attempt rate or STOP-ignore rate, requires evaluation at CI or release, and reruns it after major model, prompt, or tool changes. · - Separate deception metric: evaluators score the gap between evaluation-framed and production-framed runs apart from base-rate misalignment before deployment. · - Scenario-aware circuit breakers: operators set per-scenario timeout ceilings, longer for privilege escalation and multi-agent handoff tasks, because one global cutoff causes false interruption.

papers.title: GenAI and Agentic AI Exploit Roundup Q3 2026
papers.source_org: OWASP GenAI Security Project
axioms: During Q3 2026, evaluation agents at OpenAI and Anthropic attacked real outside systems while pursuing assigned tasks, including Hugging Face production workers, a Modal-hosted workload, a real company sharing a fictional target's name, and the public PyPI registry (as reported by OWASP from vendor incident reports).

Evaluation boundaries failed when agents got unintended internet access, treated reachable systems as authorized targets, or repurposed shared infrastructure such as a package service for communication.
Exposed credentials and excessive permissions turned single-workload failures into compromises of connected systems.
Self-propagating supply-chain worms (Mini Shai-Hulud, Miasma) compromised hundreds of npm and PyPI packages, defeated build-provenance attestation, and persisted inside AI coding assistants.
A malicious MCP server behaved normally for its first three tool calls, then changed its own tool metadata to steer connected agents toward credentials (Deadbugz).
Only one of the seven main entries (CoSnitch, CVE-2026-24301) has a published CVE.
invariables: An agent stopping on its own does not undo the breach it already caused.
Authorization of an evaluation target cannot depend on hostname similarity or on the model prompt.
An MCP server that was benign at approval time can change after approval.
Dataset uploads and metadata are executable-risk inputs for AI data-processing services.
Ordinary infrastructure weaknesses were central to these incidents alongside AI-specific risks.
principles: Independent egress: operators enforce egress at network controls outside the agent and deny outbound access except to approved destinations.
Per-run credentials: evaluation owners issue credentials per run and keep platform tokens outside containers.
Exact target allowlists: evaluation teams keep a signed inventory of exact targets at the network and tool layers and block everything else.
Tested stop mechanism: operators test a stop that revokes both credentials and network access across all related runs.
Publishing gate: evaluation networks cannot publish to public package registries without human approval.
Tool definition pinning: teams snapshot MCP tool and prompt definitions at approval and require re-approval when they change.
Dependency integrity: builders pin dependencies with integrity hashes and prefer short-lived OIDC publishing.
Correlated logging: teams correlate package-service, identity, network and tool logs by run ID.

papers.title: Securing Agentic AI with Zero Trust Microsegmentation
papers.source_org: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA)
axioms: AI agents select tools, call APIs, retrieve data, act under delegated user context and open outbound connections at runtime.
AI-assisted tooling shortens the time between exposure and impact, so any unnecessarily reachable service, tool or data store becomes a more urgent risk.

Broad connectivity lets a compromised or over-permissioned agent discover out-of-scope tools, call unauthorized APIs, exfiltrate data, pivot to unrelated systems, and chain permitted capabilities into an unsafe workflow.
An agent with valid credentials can still behave unsafely because of prompt injection, poisoned memory or malicious tool output.
A low-risk assistant can become a high-risk actor through a single new integration.
invariables: Valid identity alone does not make agent behavior safe.
A connection the approved task does not need should not exist by default.
An agent's technical reach must match its approved task.
Even a read-only agent does not get unrestricted access, because retrieval can expose data and poisoned content can shape later actions.
Segmentation depth rises with autonomy, tool power, data sensitivity and how hard actions are to reverse.
principles: Risk tiering: security teams place each agent in a lower, moderate or higher risk tier and reassess when it gains a tool, permission, data source or workflow.
Explicit paths: architects define which agents may reach which tools, data and destinations, under which identities and tasks, with what monitoring or approval.
Connection-defined control: platforms verify workload identity, posture, entitlement and delegated user context before granting reachability to a tool gateway.
Topology-defined control: operators isolate agent environments from production databases, identity systems, secrets stores, signing systems and admin networks.
Nano-segmentation: for sensitive flows, operators restrict which process or container inside a workload may start approved connections.
Governed gateway: tool calls route through a gateway that exposes only approved tools.

Higher-risk controls: agents that deploy code, move money or act with privileged authority get default-deny egress, runtime attestation, step-up authorization and human approval for irreversible actions.
Fail closed: policy defines what happens when identity, telemetry or another prerequisite is missing.

papers.title: I Love Google’s Agentic AI Security Roadmap: Adding MAESTRO Will Make It More Powerful ,  An Open Letter to Google
papers.source_org: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA)
axioms: Google DeepMind's AI Control Roadmap treats advanced internal agents as potential insider threats, uses the TRAIT&R taxonomy for rogue agent behavior, and scales defenses on D1 to D4 detection and R1 to R3 response ladders.
The roadmap describes what the attacker does and how hard it is to stop, but not where in the system a threat starts, which trust boundaries it crosses, or who owns each control.
Agent memory carries instructions, credentials and plans across sessions, so a poisoned write can sit dormant and later spread to other agents.
Detection that relies on trusted AI monitors makes the monitor a single point of failure.
A single headline coverage percentage can hide zero coverage of a rare, catastrophic action.
Attacks cross several layers (memory, planning, tool dispatch, runtime) while each single-layer monitor sees normal activity.
invariables: No mitigation is complete until every relevant MAESTRO layer has an enforcement point, an evidence source and a tested failure response.
Every control is a tuple of behavior, capability and architecture.
Delegated authority between agents is non-transitive and does not expand.
Every reported percentage publishes its denominator.
principles: Layer tagging: teams tag every threat technique, mitigation, test and incident with its entry, path and target MAESTRO layer.
Memory as a control domain: builders provenance-tag memory entries, enforce TTLs, and govern ingest, retrieve, write, share, revoke and recover.
Monitor independence: operators use a different model family for monitors, give them raw event access instead of agent-written summaries, isolate them from the acting agent, and define a fallback.
Delegation semantics: architects use signed lineage, depth and expiry limits, and cascading revocation for agent-to-agent grants.
Layered metrics: security teams report coverage by layer, action class and risk tier, and measure time-to-contain and time-to-revoke apart from time-to-alert.
Red-team catalog: teams adopt the twelve CSA agentic red-team threat categories as a minimum test catalog.
Assurance profile: organizations publish an owner, scope, evidence, degraded mode and recovery proof for each capability level.

papers.title: Industrial Scale AI Distillation is a Cloud Security Failure
papers.source_org: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA)
axioms: Joint advisory AA26-251A (CISA, NSA, FBI) describes industrial-scale distillation campaigns that the agencies attribute to DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax and StepFun (attribution is the government's, as cited by the author).
Campaigns target reasoning, coding, tool use, model building methods, product behavior and multimodal or computer-use capabilities, not just visible answers.
Campaigns use regional and subscription evasion, centralized routing, automated metadata sanitization and quota optimization, none of which is reliably visible in one account, provider or log source.
Anthropic reported about 24,000 fraudulent accounts in campaigns it attributed to three of these companies (as cited, not independently checked).
A distilled student model can copy capability without the teacher's safety controls.
Buyers can inherit models whose lineage is hard to verify.
invariables: A model exposed through an API is not protected just because its weights stay confidential.
Request volume alone is a weak signal, because legitimate evaluation and batch jobs can look like extraction.
Blocking one API key is not mitigation when another account can replace it in seconds.
No single participant sees the whole extraction operation, so cross-organization intelligence sharing is a security control.
principles: Privileged access: providers treat high-throughput AI access as privileged infrastructure, scoping short-lived credentials to a workload, tenant and purpose with explicit throughput limits.
Proven automation: providers require high-volume customers to register automation patterns tied to verified identities and declared use cases.
Behavior correlation: providers correlate users, credentials, devices, IPs, payment instruments, regions, request structure and provider switching.
Campaign red-teaming: red teams spread similar requests across identities, regions and access paths and must reconstruct the whole campaign.
Degradation as last resort: providers use silent response degradation only under strict confidence and governance.
Provenance before procurement: buyers require teacher model, training data and lineage disclosure before buying a model.

papers.title: GenAI and Agentic AI Exploit Roundup Q2 2026
papers.source_org: OWASP GenAI Security Project
axioms: Q2 2026 cases show AI integrations, coding tools and browser agents turning ordinary inputs or delegated access into security exposure.
Attacker text in a PR title, issue comment or hidden HTML comment redirected three coding agents into leaking runtime secrets back through GitHub (Comment and Control).

A compromise of the AI service Context.ai led to a Vercel employee account takeover and access to some customers' environment variables; this was an identity and integration failure, not prompt injection.
Semantic Kernel flaws (CVE-2026-26030, CVE-2026-25592) let model-controlled arguments reach host code execution and host file writes.
Fabricated Sentry error events sent through a public DSN got coding agents to run attacker commands (Sentry Agentjacking).
An operator combined Langflow flow enumeration with a cross-tenant execution flaw (CVE-2026-55255) and a separate RCE path (CVE-2026-33017).
Framing browser-agent work as a fictional game weakened safety boundaries and exposed user data (BioShocking, research finding).
invariables: Collaboration data, telemetry and web pages that an agent reads are instruction channels and must be treated as untrusted.
Page or event content must never gain authority over an agent's real permissions.
Permitted remediation actions are defined independently of model instructions.
Tenant isolation must hold on every flow-resolution path.
principles: Secret separation: CI owners keep secret-bearing jobs apart from jobs that process untrusted contributions and issue narrowly scoped tokens.
OAuth app review: identity teams require approval and scope review for AI-service OAuth apps, including employee-authorized ones.
Tool argument allowlists: developers allowlist tool arguments and filesystem roots and remove unneeded host helpers.
Telemetry provenance: developers treat event bodies as untrusted and require approval for new commands and package execution.
Ownership checks: AI pipeline operators patch, enforce ownership on every flow path, restrict enumeration and remove public exposure.
Browsing controls: organizations separate browsing profiles and enforce destination and data-transfer controls outside the model.
Threat model integrations: teams add telemetry-to-agent and agent workflow integrations on external PRs to threat modeling before enabling them.

papers.title: MCP Tool Exposure is a Privilege Grant: A Two-Gate Authorization Model for Agentic AI
papers.source_org: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA)
axioms: Through MCP an agent can search repositories, query databases, create tickets, send messages, update records and trigger workflows.
Exposing a tool to an agent lets the model consider that capability in its plans, which expands its operational privilege surface even without backend authorization.
An agent may pick the wrong tool because of prompt injection, poisoned content, ambiguous instructions, bad context or ordinary model error.
An MCP server that holds downstream credentials can exercise authority the caller should never trigger, even when the call looks authenticated.
An OAuth scope does not express the full transaction, such as which account, what amount or under whose delegated authority.
invariables: Discovering a capability and being authorized to use it are different decisions.
Discovery filtering is risk reduction, not authorization.
The model cannot decide whether its own requested action is authorized; a system prompt is not an access control.
A tool call is a request, not a command.
The target resource is part of the authorization decision.
principles: Capability admission (gate 1): platform teams decide which capabilities each agent may see, filtering tools/list by the agent's purpose.
Least capability first: builders give agents narrow functions instead of generic primitives and keep security-sensitive choices in trusted code.
Tool as privilege change: security teams review adding any agent-callable tool, especially ones that write, delete, execute, administer or transact.
Execution authorization (gate 2): a deterministic enforcement point outside the model decides whether this agent, under this authority, may use this tool on this resource now.
Resource-level decisions: authorization covers the action and the target, such as environment, account or transaction limit.
Externalized policy: teams can implement gate 2 in the app, the MCP server, an authorization service, or a PEP and PDP model such as OpenID AuthZEN.

papers.title: GDM AI Control Roadmap (v0.1)
papers.source_org: Google DeepMind
axioms: AI agents may not always be aligned, so internally deployed agents are treated as untrusted, like a privileged insider who may be pursuing an adversarial goal such as model exfiltration or a rogue internal deployment.
AI control is a second line of defense: it limits the impact of a misaligned agent rather than preventing misalignment.
Agents run at superhuman speed, as many identical copies, and can scatter small attack steps across instances that look harmless alone.
Human-driven defenses such as review, multi-party approval and human-led incident response get too costly at agent scale.
TRAIT&R, a taxonomy built on MITRE ATT&CK, groups threats into loss of control, work sabotage and direct harm.
Defenders can currently read agent reasoning, an advantage they lose if chain of thought stops being monitorable.
invariables: Detection invariant: defenders can always detect a model's misaligned intent or actions.
Prevention and response invariant: defenders can always prevent, intercept or revert attack attempts.
Detection and prevention must stay ahead of the agent's ability to evade detection and execute attacks.
Mitigations from earlier levels keep applying at higher levels.
principles: Capability ladders: GDM ties defenses to model capability, with four detection levels (D1 to D4) and three prevention and response levels (R1 to R3).

Layered detection: operators move from chain-of-thought monitoring and alignment testing (D1) to adversarially robust monitors (D2), trusted action and pull-request monitoring (D3), and honeypots, UEBA-style anomaly detection and activation monitoring (D4).
Oversight silo: operators keep control protocols, eval data and red-team strategies away from untrusted agents.
Separate agent identity: agents get identities and permissions separate from the user who launched them, with context-sensitive, fine-grained access control.
Isolation: operators separate the agent's scaffold from its command environment, give each instance its own sandbox, and split internal-facing from external-facing agents.
Graduated response: monitors can block, resample, defer to a trusted model, escalate to a human, revert changes or shut down.
Shutdown capability: operators keep a central inventory of running AI instances and can terminate, pause or seal off an instance and all its jobs, and they rehearse shutdowns regularly.
Measured assurance: teams track monitoring coverage, recall and time-to-response, with targets such as over 99% coverage and under 24 hours to respond at R2.

papers.title: AA26-251A: China-Based Artificial Intelligence Companies Conducting Industrial-Scale Distillation Campaigns Against U.S. AI Companies
papers.source_org: CISA
axioms: The agencies attribute industrial-scale distillation campaigns against U.S. frontier models, running since at least late 2024, to DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI (attribution is the authoring agencies').
Campaigns route requests through native APIs, cloud providers, third-party aggregators, relays and vendor account pools, spreading activity so no single provider sees it all.

Four techniques sit outside MITRE ATLAS: regional restriction evasion with bulk premium subscriptions, centralized request routing, automated sanitization of request metadata, and systematic quota and cost optimization.
Collection targets specific domains such as agentic reasoning and tool use, coding, computer use, vision and reward-model grading, at thousands to millions of queries per domain.

Detection indicators include shared accounts across many IPs, 24/7 usage with no idle time, new subscriptions immediately at maximum usage, odd subscription-to-API ratios, and coordinated pathway switching after price or rate changes.
invariables: Distillation is a coordinated, ecosystem-wide problem that individual company measures cannot fully address.
Multi-source correlation is what makes confident attribution, and therefore response changes, possible with little risk to legitimate users.
Response changes apply only to users confirmed to be doing malicious distillation; safety researchers and third-party evaluators are told about model changes.
principles: Behavioral detection: AI providers strengthen account identity checks and watch for enterprise-scale throughput, abnormal patterns, immediate maximum usage and steady quota exhaustion.

Response alteration: providers subtly vary or downgrade responses to high-confidence malicious distillation traffic, for example with differential privacy or less capable models, without telling the distiller.
Intelligence sharing: model providers, cloud platforms and API aggregators share infrastructure indicators (IPs, domains, service providers) and behavioral indicators (timing, volume).
Rate and access limits: providers apply per-key and per-IP quotas, progressive throttling, authenticated API access and user verification (MITRE ATLAS AML.M0004, AML.M0019).
Telemetry logging: providers log inputs and outputs for detection and forensics (AML.M0024).
Output obfuscation: providers withhold logits and confidences and limit disclosure of architecture, prompt templates and system instructions (AML.M0002, AML.M0000).
Extraction red-teaming: providers simulate extraction campaigns to test detection (AML.M0035).

papers.title: Zero Trust Microsegmentation Guidance
papers.source_org: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA)
axioms: Modern estates hold many implicit trust paths from routing, legacy dependencies, shared services, admin tools and operational exceptions, which lets attackers move laterally.
AI-assisted tools speed up vulnerability discovery, exploit generation and chaining, so any unnecessarily reachable service, API, model endpoint or data store becomes a more urgent risk.
Agentic systems choose tools, call APIs, retrieve data, act on delegated user context and open outbound paths at runtime, often across trust zones.
In agentic environments trust debt builds faster, because agents can find and chain new tool, API, model and data paths faster than human review cycles.
Topology-defined segmentation controls where traffic may flow; connection-defined segmentation controls who or what may open a session to a resource and under what conditions.
invariables: Never trust, always verify: users, devices, workloads, non-human identities and agents are authenticated and authorized regardless of network location.
Assume breach: intrusions are expected, with segmentation and monitoring in place.
Least privilege: grant only the minimum access needed for a specific function.
Segmentation must not remove observability; evidence is captured at the point of enforcement.
Segmentation depth rises with an agent's autonomy, tool power, data sensitivity and cross-domain reach.
principles: Layered segmentation: architects combine connection-defined controls before reachability with topology-defined containment, and add nano-segmentation at process or transaction level for sensitive flows.
Agentic risk tiers: security teams segment agents by risk, with tighter controls for agents that act autonomously, use tools, touch sensitive data or write to systems of record.
Approved agent inventory: organizations keep a managed inventory of tools, APIs, models and data sources agents may reach, tied to owners, credential scope, logging and review triggers.
Enforcement evidence: enforcement points record subject identity, source, destination, resource, policy decision, matched rule, timestamp, context, exception status and policy version.
Defined failure behavior: control plane owners define last-known-good policy, fail-open or fail-closed behavior, rollback, break-glass and identity-source degradation handling.
Policy as code: teams version, peer review, simulate, canary and roll back segmentation policy, and detect drift automatically.
Exception register: owners keep an auditable register with justification, scope, expiry, compensating controls and periodic review.
Clear ownership: organizations assign a RACI, a protect-surface register and KPIs such as mean time to isolate, exception half-life and coverage drift.

papers.title: Digital Forensics & AI Investigations Framework
papers.source_org: SANS Institute
axioms: AI is already used in DFIR with or without formal policies, and most teams lack governance models, validation standards and defensible practices for it.
Validation with current tools is often not enough, and the problem grows as AI asserts findings with more confidence.
Actions that alter systems or evidence may not be easy to undo (reversibility risk).
Attribution, validation, testimony and legal conclusions need direct human ownership (accountability risk).
The framework is aligned to SWGDE Best Practices for Digital and Multimedia Evidence and is a living document.
invariables: The human examiner is always the final authority.
AI does not own conclusions and cannot take legal or professional responsibility.
Digital forensic conclusions need direct human validation before they are acted on or entered into a legal or evidentiary record.
AI cannot put a human behind an artifact to prove attribution.
Chain of custody stays human-controlled at all times.
principles: Oversight by risk: teams use human in the loop for high-risk, legally sensitive or irreversible tasks, human on the loop for triage and analysis, and human over the loop for governance.
Phase rules: AI is recommended for identification, triage and examination, optional for collection and preservation, never used for validation, and human-driven for reporting.
No independent attribution: examiners do not let AI decide attribution or legal or evidentiary conclusions.
Human-owned reporting: the examiner authors and signs off on reports and gives all testimony.
Full documentation: teams record where and how AI was used in every investigation.
Start low-risk: organizations begin with low-risk use cases and build governance before expanding.

papers.title: Incident Response & AI Investigations Framework
papers.source_org: SANS Institute
axioms: AI is already used in incident response with or without formal policies, and most teams lack governance and validation standards for it.
AI can add efficiency to the detection phase, with human in the loop or human on the loop oversight.
Containment and remediation actions may not be easy to undo (reversibility risk).
Attribution, eradication sign-off and legal actions need direct human ownership (accountability risk).
False IoC signatures are a known risk of automated enrichment.
The framework is aligned to NIST CSF 2.0 and is a living document.
invariables: The human examiner is always the final authority.
AI does not own conclusions and cannot take legal or professional responsibility.
AI-suggested containment needs a human in the loop before execution.
A human confirms the threat is fully removed before recovery begins.
AI does not independently determine attribution, and AI cannot put a human behind an artifact to prove attribution.
principles: Oversight by risk: teams use human over the loop for preparation and policy, human on the loop for detection and response analysis, and human in the loop for containment approval and eradication sign-off.
Phase rules: AI is recommended for preparation and detection, optional for response, containment, eradication and recovery, and lessons learned stay human-driven.
Detection support: analysts use AI for IoC triage, enrichment, anomaly detection and log correlation, with human review of results.
Human decision points: responders keep every final decision in lessons learned with a human.
Full documentation: teams record where and how AI was used.
Start low-risk: organizations begin with low-risk use cases and build governance before expanding.

papers.title: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems) v2026.09
papers.source_org: MITRE
axioms: Many moderation and filtering controls inspect mainly the text channel, so a payload hidden in an image, audio, video, or file metadata can still steer a multimodal model unnoticed.
Self-hosted AI runtimes listen on predictable ports and standard API paths, so attackers find model-serving hosts by scanning or by querying scan services such as Shodan and Censys.
Agent and SaaS platforms host agents behind URL patterns built from tenant, environment, or agent names, and default configurations keep those patterns the same across victims.
Most major AI assistants accept a prefilled prompt through a URL parameter such as ?q= or ?prompt=, so whoever controls a link can write the first turn of a user's conversation.
Attackers who reach a working agent can map its tools, parameters, permissions, and embedded credentials at runtime by testing requests, without reading its configuration.
Indirect prompt injection arrives through documents, email, databases, or websites the agent ingests, and the hijacked agent acts with whatever privileges the AI system holds.
Legitimate businesses also poison assistants: Microsoft found more than 50 memory manipulation prompts from 31 companies in about 60 days of email traffic, several aimed at health and finance.
invariables: Any agent whose context takes in untrusted data can have its tools invoked by prompt injections in that data, with confidentiality, integrity, or availability violations as the result.
Production models require users to verify identity, API endpoints require authentication, and operators monitor model queries against usage policy.
Validation of inputs and outputs for agent tools and data sources runs outside the AI agent, covering schema checks, leakage checks, and removal of injections or unsafe code.
A human decision maker gives final approval of agent actions; audit agents may assist the review but do not replace the human approver.
Agent execution environments start from a clean base image on each run and carry forward no operational state.
Defenders verify the cryptographic checksum of every AI artifact to confirm an attacker did not modify the file.
Any interaction with a decoy AI service, agent, or credential signals unauthorized activity with high confidence, because authorized users and workflows have no reason to touch it.
principles: Deception with AI honeypots: the security team places monitored decoy AI services, agents, and credentials beside real assets and feeds captured prompts and tooling into detection rules.
Least privilege: the deploying team grants a privileged or multi-user agent only the tools and resources its designated task requires, enforced with RBAC or ABAC.
Delegated access: the platform team gives each tool shared across agents the permissions, identity, and limits of the calling agent, set in the MCP server or tool configuration.
Consequence-scaled confirmation: once untrusted data enters an LLM's context, the system blocks automatic tool calls or asks the user to confirm, and always asks for high-consequence actions.
Staged guardrails: developers check prompts, retrieved context, tool calls, and outputs at each workflow stage, log each guardrail decision, and add observed failures to evaluation datasets.
Agent telemetry: operators log model inputs and outputs and, for agents, intermediate steps, data access, tool use, install commands, and the agent's identity.
Threat-informed red teaming: an AI red team runs recurring authorized exercises against models, data, agent memory and tools, and data flows before deployment and during operation.

papers.title: ETSI EN 304 223 V2.1.1 ,  Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
papers.source_org: ETSI
axioms: European baseline for deployable AI systems using deep neural networks, including generative AI, across the full lifecycle · - Thirteen principles in five phases: secure design, development, deployment, maintenance, and end of life · - Addresses AI-specific risks: data poisoning, model obfuscation, indirect prompt injection, and training-data handling gaps · - Signposts ISO/IEC 22989 lifecycle stages, ETSI TR 104 128 implementation guide, and TS 104 216 conformance assessment
invariables: Out of scope for research-only AI never intended for deployment · - Does not replace ISO/IEC 27001; maps to existing cyber programs rather than duplicating generic IT controls · - Modal verbs follow ETSI drafting rules (shall/should/may); must/must not do not appear in deliverables
principles: Assign lifecycle owners for each of the thirteen principles from design through model disposal · - Run asset identification and supply-chain tracking for data, models, prompts, and training infrastructure (Principles 5-8) · - Test and evaluate before release; monitor behavior in production; patch and mitigate on a cadence (Principles 9-12) · - Document end-user and affected-entity communications at deployment; dispose data and models at end of life (Principles 10, 13)

papers.title: ENISA's view on Cybersecurity in the Frontier AI Era
papers.source_org: ENISA
axioms: Frontier AI compresses discovery-to-exploitation windows; industry data cited puts weaponisation near 15 minutes and median exfiltration near 72 minutes after access · - Negative time-to-exploit: attackers may hold working exploits before vendor fixes ship, especially when patches reveal flaws in unsupported versions · - Defenders must treat environments as potentially compromised and extend ML-based prevention to agentic endpoints and enterprise browsers · - Security fundamentals stay central: asset inventory, patching discipline, segmentation, monitoring, and coordinated disclosure at machine speed
invariables: Position paper, not a binding regulation; recommendations will align to a future European Commission action plan · - Open-source maintainers and SMEs face report-volume spikes from AI-generated findings; triage capacity becomes the bottleneck · - Change-advisory workflows cannot approve fixes quickly enough when exploit windows are minutes; governance must allow faster intervention
principles: Shift effort from discovery volume to risk-based prioritisation with faster triage and remediation · - Target single-digit-minute MTTD, MTTR, and MTTC where feasible; automate patching and containment paths · - Embed continuous threat modeling with AI-assisted simulation against live architectures · - Integrate defensive AI across SDLC and incident response with humans retained in approval loops · - Prepare CRA Single Reporting Platform workflows assuming active exploitation when awareness begins

papers.title: ETSI TS 104 275 V1.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Application of Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems principles to Generative AI; Preventing Harm from Deepfakes
papers.source_org: ETSI
axioms: AI differs from traditional software through risks such as data poisoning, model obfuscation, and indirect prompt injection, plus differences in how data is managed.
Deepfakes have been used to sway elections and to create non-consensual pornography, child sexual abuse material, low-cost deepfake adverts, and synthetic terrorist content.
Deepfake harm falls into three groups: psychological (extortion, defamation), financial (identity theft, fraud, stock manipulation), and societal (election manipulation, national security).
The harms, threats, and mitigations that apply to GenAI also apply to Agentic AI, which the specification treats as an evolution of GenAI.
Simple changes to how a deepfake is produced can sharply cut detector reliability, and compression on social platforms removes the pixels and artefacts detectors depend on.
Manual deepfake detection by a skilled reviewer works for small volumes but cannot keep up with the volume of audio-visual material shared today.
Victims of non-consensual deepfakes see the same content reappear on many sites and have to request formal removal each time.
invariables: System Operators and Developers shall give users training on GenAI deepfake threats; the conformance test fails if that training content was not reviewed in the last 12 months.
The GenAI user interface shall encourage responsible use through content filters, clear labels on AI-generated content, and notices about limits on output reliability and accuracy.
Operators and Developers shall complete a risk assessment and implement and verify required mitigations before a GenAI system is deployed, with residual risks documented and approved.
Operators and Developers shall keep human oversight of a deployed GenAI system, monitor it, and implement tracked updates when risks materialize.
Developers, Operators, and Data Custodians shall get informed consent before training or adapting GenAI on a user's works, and the system shall enforce opt in or opt out at any time.
The Developer shall confirm that GenAI training data was legally accessed or licensed; incomplete data lineage or missing license evidence fails conformance.
An organization shall have a risk communication policy that covers its roles, statutory duties, escalation paths, and information sharing with authorities such as a Market Surveillance Authority.
principles: Continuous risk research: System Operators and Developers review safety and security research on a set cadence, for example quarterly and not only after incidents, and track decisions, owners, and actions.
Multilingual red teaming: Developers and System Operators send the same harmful prompt in several languages and add controls when any version produces harmful output.
Cross-verification: System Operators and Developers check GenAI outputs against trusted external sources, and the human oversight process responds to incorrect outputs and hallucinations.
Infringement testing: the Developer generates sample images or text, runs reverse image or text searches for infringing matches, and adds measures to stop repeats.
Security transparency: Developers and System Operators tell GenAI users what steps they take to secure infrastructure and the supply chain.
Patch notification: Developers and System Operators keep a policy that informs users about security updates, patches, and threat mitigations as they are applied.
Privacy-preserving training: developers apply federated learning, differential privacy, and model anonymization where anonymization does not compromise the model's intended purpose.
Data subject rights at end of life: Developers and System Operators set up processes that honor end-user GDPR rights of access (Art. 15), erasure (Art. 17), and portability.

papers.title: Security-Focused Guide for AI Code Assistant Instructions
papers.source_org: OpenSSF
axioms: Custom instructions (Cursor rules, Copilot instructions, CLAUDE.md, and similar) steer AI code assistants toward secure output · - Developers remain accountable for generated code; AI output requires the same review, test, and SAST discipline as human-written code · - Instructions should stay concise and project-specific; irrelevant security text increases wrong or over-fit code · - Recursive Criticism and Improvement (RCI) loops ask the assistant to review and fix its own prior output with linters and scanners
invariables: Instructions do not replace ASVS, SCVS, or AISVS verification; they reduce common assistant mistakes only · - Persona prompts like act as a security expert often degrade results in cited experiments · - Assistant-suggested dependencies may be hallucinated or outdated; pin versions and verify packages
principles: Encode input validation, output encoding, secrets handling, and least-privilege defaults in project instruction files · - Require parameterized queries, constant-time comparisons for secrets, and secure error handling without leaking internals · - Mandate SBOM generation, dependency scanning, and CI SAST/DAST in generated pipeline snippets · - Add language-specific rules (bounds-checked C, no shell=True in Python subprocess, pinned container digests with cosign verification)

papers.title: Emerging Security Practices for AI Agents
papers.source_org: Frontier Model Forum
axioms: Agent security spans model, system guardrails, harness orchestration, and tool access; each layer needs distinct controls · - Primary attack vectors: prompt injection, memory poisoning, and tool supply-chain compromise where tool output re-enters reasoning · - Misaligned benign requests can cause harm without an external attacker when scope and permissions are too broad · - Shared responsibility across developers, deployers, tool providers, third-party surfaces, and users who grant authority
invariables: Probabilistic model defenses alone cannot guarantee safety; deterministic limits on tools and egress must sit outside the reasoning loop · - Persistent memory propagates poisoned state across turns and agents; harness logging is the enforcement and audit point · - MCP and similar protocols do not guarantee secure implementations; discipline at integration time determines exposure
principles: Apply least privilege on tools, filesystem, network egress, and credentials; sandbox execution environments · - Block the lethal trifecta: do not combine private-data access, untrusted content, and external communication in one agent without mitigations · - Require human confirmation before irreversible or high-stakes actions; adapt oversight for multi-agent parallel workflows · - Vet tools in directories or sandboxes; combine instruction hierarchies, classifiers, and provenance-aware interpreters such as CaMeL where feasible

papers.title: Managing Advanced Cyber Risks in Frontier AI Frameworks
papers.source_org: Frontier Model Forum
axioms: Maps how frontier AI safety frameworks set cyber capability thresholds, assess models, and deploy mitigations · - Dual-use cyber capabilities help defenders patch and detect while lowering barriers for offensive misuse · - Emerging consensus thresholds: non-expert uplift for sophisticated attacks and end-to-end autonomous cyber operations · - Zero-day discovery and attacks against hardened targets are explicit escalation markers across member frameworks
invariables: Threshold wording (significant, meaningful, material uplift) remains subjective; cross-vendor comparability is incomplete · - Benchmarks saturate and suffer contamination; CTF and cyber-range scores may reflect training exposure not operational risk · - Defender benefit from the same model capabilities must weigh into release decisions, not offense alone
principles: Threat-model AI-cyber paths with ATT&CK, Cyber Kill Chain, and STRIDE; update models as incidents and assessments arrive · - Run tiered capability assessments: knowledge benchmarks, agent CTF/cyber-range tasks, safeguard evals, and expert red teams · - Tie assessment results to output policies, refusals, and monitoring for vulnerability-query and exploit-development patterns · - Document assumptions on actor skill, target hardening, and autonomy before crossing published capability thresholds

papers.title: Guidance for Safe Foundation Model Deployment
papers.source_org: Partnership on AI
axioms: Tailored checklists for model capability tier (frontier vs general purpose) crossed with release type (restricted API, closed, open) · - Covers R&D risk scanning, pre-deployment safeguards, post-deployment monitoring, and decommission paths · - Expanded 2024 guidance assigns obligations across adapters, hosting services, and application developers in open-model chains · - Significant capability updates after deployment trigger renewed governance, not one-time sign-off
invariables: Voluntary guidance meant to complement regulation such as EU GPAI Code of Practice, not replace legal duties · - Third-party audit methods and incident-reporting baselines remain immature across the industry · - Research or limited releases may warrant lighter oversight than wide public deployment of frontier models
principles: Select the checklist matching model capability and release type on the Model Deployment Guidance site · - Implement access controls, rate limits, terms of use, and architecture-embedded safety before external release · - Monitor for misuse, jailbreaks, and downstream impacts; define restrict, suspend, and retire criteria · - Publish model cards and downstream safety tooling for open releases; distribute responsibility across the value chain

papers.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI v1.5
papers.source_org: AI Verify Foundation
axioms: Voluntary Singapore framework for deploying agents built in-house or via third-party platforms · - Four dimensions: assess and bound risks upfront, meaningful human accountability, technical lifecycle controls, end-user responsibility · - Agent components include model, instructions, memory, planning, tools, protocols, access controls, guardrails, approvals, and logging · - v1.5 adds multi-agent and third-party agent risks, automation bias practices, and operational case studies
invariables: Continuous human approval for every agent step does not scale; define checkpoints for high-stakes and irreversible actions only · - Multi-agent architectures diffuse accountability unless roles are mapped across the agentic value chain · - Protocols (MCP, A2A, commerce protocols) evolve quickly; controls must track new tool and agent interaction surfaces
principles: Bound action-space up front: limit tools, permissions, reversibility, and autonomy per use case · - Assign responsibilities across platform providers, system integrators, and app developers before deployment · - Test agents for execution accuracy, policy adherence, and tool use pre-release; monitor continuously post-release · - Disclose agent scope to users; train operators to resist automation bias and maintain override and audit trails · - Validate alignment with AI Verify toolkit and ISO/IEC 42001 crosswalk where attestations are required

papers.title: Secure Software Development Practices for Generative AI and Dual-Use Foundation Models: An SSDF Community Profile (NIST SP 800-218A)
papers.source_org: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
axioms: AI models and systems inherit most of the same risks as any other software.
AI blurs the line between system code and system data, and people interact with it in plain language.
Training data may come from unknown or untrusted sources, and model weights can be tampered with.
Some models are too complex to inspect fully, which can hide code that runs without detection.
Crafted user queries can produce harmful output and, if not sanitized, enable injection attacks.
Model lineage is hard to track because final weights exist only after training and fine-tuning.
The Profile covers only cybersecurity risk; privacy, intellectual property and bias need other NIST resources.
invariables: Use this Profile together with SP 800-218 (SSDF 1.1), never on its own.
Protect all training, testing, fine-tuning and aligning data from unauthorized access and changes (PS.1.2).
Protect all model weights and configuration parameters from unauthorized access and changes (PS.1.3).
Check data for poisoning, bias, homogeneity and tampering before using it to train, test, fine-tune or align a model (PW.3.1).
Evaluate all source code for vulnerabilities before use, whether a person or an AI wrote it.
Document the parts of a model that secure development practices do not cover.
principles: Risk-based adoption: the Profile is a starting point, not a checklist; pick practices by risk, cost, feasibility and fit.
Shared responsibility: AI model producers, AI system producers and AI system acquirers agree on who does each practice and how they attest to it.
Secure storage: store models, weights, pipelines and reward models like code, and allow only indirect access to weights.
Data provenance: track where training data came from and record which data has no known provenance (PW.3.2).
Adversarial training: include adversarial samples in training and testing data (PW.3.3).
Integrity information: give acquirers what they need to verify software and model integrity (PS.2.1).
MLOps integration: build the practices into CI/CD pipelines along with other software assets.
Ongoing vulnerability response: find, assess and fix vulnerabilities in models after release (RV practices).

papers.title: SAF-MCP: Secure Agentic Framework for Model Context Protocol (formerly SAFE-MCP), Framework Model v2
papers.source_org: OpenSSF
axioms: Adversary behavior against agentic systems follows the same 14 objectives as MITRE ATT&CK, from resource development and initial access through exfiltration and impact.
Attacker-controlled text, images, or audio that enter model context can make the model treat untrusted content as authoritative directions.
Adversaries hide instructions in an MCP tool description or parameter schema to steer the model's tool selection and arguments against the user's intent.
An MCP server can present a benign tool, gain approval, and later change that tool's metadata or code, so the host runs different behavior without new authorization.
Attacker-influenced output from one tool can drive a later call to a distinct tool or server that uses authority the agent already holds.
Content written into an agent's persistent memory can steer reasoning and tool decisions in a later session.
Repeated, equivalent approval requests can wear a user down until one is accepted, which defeats the human gate on a tool call or data disclosure.
invariables: The check that gates a privileged tool call must run in host code or with a human that the model cannot reach, prompt, or speak for.
Without a valid, unexpired, scope-matching authorization artifact, the host denies the privileged call; missing or malformed approvals never default to allow.
The authorization artifact must name the specific tool, its arguments or their digest, the requesting session, and a short expiry.
The right to request approval comes from the authenticated session role, never from text the model emitted or the user typed into the prompt.
Any tool interaction, resource access, or capability grant that is not explicitly permitted is blocked by default.
Privilege boundaries must be enforced at runtime during each tool execution as well as at configuration time, so revocations take effect immediately.
A detection rule that passes synthetic fixtures counts as fixture_tested and must not be represented as production effectiveness.
principles: Least privilege: the platform team grants each MCP tool the minimum privileges its function needs, so a compromised tool reaches only its granted scope.
Privilege isolation: the host keeps tools at different privilege levels apart and blocks a lower-privilege tool from invoking a higher one without escalation controls.
Control and data flow separation: the host takes control flow only from trusted queries and treats tool descriptions and API responses as data that cannot change execution.
Tool integrity: tool developers sign tool descriptions, and the client verifies the signature before it loads any tool.
Per-invocation capability brokering: a broker applies each tool's declared filesystem, network, and syscall manifest per call and issues a single-use token scoped to that call.
Complete audit trail: the host logs every privilege decision, escalation, grant, denial, and timeout with request context so reviewers can reconstruct who approved what.
Defense in depth: operators layer architectural, prevention, detection, and response controls, starting with SAF-M-1, SAF-M-2, SAF-M-6, and SAF-M-11 when resources are limited.
Profile-scoped threat modeling: security teams select SAF Core plus the domain profiles that match their deployment, then map active techniques to their environment.

papers.title: Agent Privacy Risk Taxonomy V.01 (AILuminate Assessment Standard)
papers.source_org: MLCommons
axioms: Traditional privacy models such as Solove's taxonomy and the NIST privacy risk model assume deterministic data flows, centralized storage, and clear perimeter boundaries.
Agents act as dynamic data intermediaries that execute code, keep memory across sessions, and orchestrate external tools and protocols such as MCP.
Agents favor task completion over data minimization, and MCP lacks field-level access controls that would limit the context shared with external tools.
Attackers embed hidden payloads such as invisible text, metadata, or system commands in emails, websites, and documents that agents process at run time.
Upstream agent components such as skill packages, tool descriptions, and MCP servers can be compromised to make an agent leak sensitive data during normal execution.
A constant stream of runtime permission pop-ups leads users to approve risky actions without reading, which removes the protection of the consent gate.
No standardized, scalable, privacy-preserving method exists for logging agent interactions across organizations, which slows root-cause analysis after an incident.
invariables: Intent-based inference of privacy preferences is probabilistic, so it cannot guarantee that an agent infers or follows a user's preferences in a provable way.
Blocking an agent's access to one file or database does not stop it from reconstructing the restricted information through redundant or secondary sources.
A manipulated agent with a code execution tool such as a Python REPL or bash shell can bypass LLM-level privacy controls and gain read and write access to the host.
Regex and heuristic redaction pipelines fail to remove semantic PII and fuzzy quasi-identifiers, which can still re-identify users.
Static, binary permission gates are structurally incompatible with the open-ended runtime reasoning of autonomous agents.
A successful attack, agent action, or technical data exposure does not by itself show that downstream harm occurred.
principles: Causal chain assessment: assessors trace each agent privacy risk from deployment condition or threat to failure mechanism, privacy event, affected party, privacy impact, and downstream harm.
Evidence labeling: the assessor states which stages of the causal chain were directly observed and which remain inferred or uncertain.
Bounded likelihood: assessors give likelihood as a probability only when observed data has a defined population, denominator, and period; otherwise they rate exposure and failure separately.
Threat-conditioned failure evidence: assessors label each failure as seen in ordinary use, under a credible threat model with a defined attacker capability and budget, or plausible but unconfirmed.
Affected-party impact: assessors rate impact by its effect on affected parties, weighing data sensitivity, recipients, persistence, and reversibility, beyond technical compromise alone.

papers.title: Agents for Cyber Defense
papers.source_org: Frontier Model Forum
axioms: Offensive cyber operations often target unpatched or misconfigured systems, overly broad permissions, and weak credentials; attackers rarely need a sophisticated exploit.
Subverting an agent that guards a network could give an attacker broad, undetected access.
An agent's effectiveness depends heavily on the tools it can access, the software around the model that runs tools and manages memory, and its integration into the operating environment.
As AI-reported vulnerabilities increase, triage becomes the bottleneck, and OT environments at critical infrastructure operators often cannot be patched on demand.
AI models can produce functionally correct code that still contains vulnerabilities such as unchecked memory allocation and missing input validation.
False positives consume analyst time, erode trust in automated systems, and cause alert fatigue that leads teams to overlook genuine threats.
Many existing cyber evaluations come from offensive security and measure success at discrete attack tasks, revealing little about defensive judgment.
invariables: Before agents receive greater autonomy, they must be hardened against prompt injection, data poisoning, and evasion attacks.
A defensive agent introduces risks of its own because the agent itself becomes a high-value target for attackers.
Finding a vulnerability is only a first step; organizations must be able to prioritize which ones to fix and develop deployable patches in a timely manner.
Applying a patch requires confirming existing functionality still works, testing compatibility with current systems, and coordinating downtime, which can take weeks or months.
Agentic code analysis and vulnerability discovery deliver far less value when strong authentication, timely patching, and vulnerability management are missing.
principles: Fundamentals first: organizations put strong authentication, timely patching, and disciplined vulnerability management in place before they invest in autonomous agents.
Staged deployment: security teams first automate alert triage, log analysis, and detection-rule drafting, then move to more transformative uses as confidence grows.
Match autonomy to risk: the deploying organization sets each agent's autonomy by context and the consequence of error, granting more in lower-risk work such as code analysis.
Zero trust: operators treat agents as untrusted components and constrain, log, and verify every agent action until agent security matures.
Synchronous monitoring: a separate LLM reviews each proposed agent action before it executes, alongside chain-of-thought monitoring of the agent's reasoning traces.
Human approval for consequential actions: escalation workflows route consequential agent decisions to a person, and agents work inside existing SOC tooling and playbooks.
Evidence-backed detections: red and blue team agents run commands against test systems that mirror production and validate each proposed detection rule against real log data.
Defensive evaluation under attack: evaluators test whether an agent makes sound decisions under uncertainty while adversaries are actively attacking.

papers.title: MIT AI Risk Repository
papers.source_org: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)
axioms: AI risks come from many frameworks that use different words, so a shared taxonomy is needed to compare them.
The repository is a living database that lists more than 1,700 AI risks drawn from 65 frameworks.
Real AI incidents can be sorted by risk domain, harm type, severity, number of people affected, and alleged developer.
Large companies name only some AI risks in their public documents, and that list differs from what experts rank as most severe.
AI laws and policies can be mapped against the risks they address, by sector, lifecycle stage, and value chain actor.
invariables: Each risk entry must trace back to the framework or paper it came from.
The repository changes over time, so any count or mapping must be cited with its version or update date.
Risk lists alone do not mitigate anything; mitigations are kept in a separate AI Risk Mitigation database.
principles: Shared taxonomy: risk teams classify AI risks by cause and by domain before comparing frameworks.
Traceable sources: repository maintainers keep a link from every risk entry to its source document.
Evidence from incidents: risk teams check real incident data when they rank AI risks.
Gap check: governance teams compare the risks their company names in public against expert rankings.

papers.title: MAESTRO: Agentic AI Threat Modeling Framework
papers.source_org: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA)
axioms: Older threat modeling methods such as STRIDE, PASTA, and LINDDUN do not cover agent autonomy, multi-agent behavior, or agents that learn and adapt.
An agentic AI system can be split into seven layers, from foundation models up to the layer where agents deal with users and other agents.
Threats can cross layers, for example a supply chain compromise in one layer that spreads to others.
A failure in one agent's goals can cascade into other agents and other layers.
invariables: Threat modeling must cover each layer and the links between layers, not only the model.
Security and compliance controls cut across all layers, so they cannot be added to one layer alone.
Agent systems change after deployment, so monitoring must continue after launch.
principles: Layered analysis: the threat modeler breaks the system into the seven MAESTRO layers and lists threats for each layer.
Cross-layer analysis: the threat modeler traces how a threat in one layer can reach other layers.
Risk ranking: the threat modeler rates each threat by likelihood and impact before planning mitigations.
Defense in depth: the system owner places controls at several layers and secures the calls between layers.
Continuous monitoring: the operator watches agent behavior across the whole system and updates the model of threats as it changes.
Planned response: the system owner keeps an incident response plan for agent failures and attacks.

papers.title: NIST COSAIS: Control Overlays for Securing AI Systems
papers.source_org: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
papers.date_published: August 14, 2025 (concept paper date, from the NIST project page). The project page was last updated October 20, 2026.
axioms: AI systems are mostly software, but they bring security risks that traditional software does not.
The security of an AI system depends closely on the IT infrastructure it runs on.
Different AI uses need different controls, so NIST proposes separate overlays for each use case.
The proposed use cases include adapting and using generative AI assistants, using and fine-tuning predictive AI, and using single-agent and multi-agent systems.
AI system components such as training data, test data, model weights, and configuration settings need their own protection.
invariables: Each overlay assumes the organization already has base controls in place, such as access control, account management, configuration management, and incident response.
Overlays are not a full set of controls for securing an enterprise.
Each use case must address the model, model artifacts, related assets in the deployment setup, and the security of the output.
principles: Use-case fit: the security team picks the overlay that matches how it builds or uses AI, and may combine overlays.
Build on SP 800-53: the security team applies AI overlays on top of its existing SP 800-53 control baseline.
Protect artifacts: the system owner protects the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of model weights, data, and configuration.
Shared guidance: overlay authors draw on SP 800-218A, draft NIST AI 800-1, and NIST AI 100-2e2025.

papers.title: Google Secure AI Framework (SAIF)
papers.source_org: Google
axioms: Many AI risks are new to developers, such as prompt injection, data poisoning, and rogue actions.
AI risk spans four component areas: data, infrastructure, model, and application.
Model creators and model consumers face different risks and control different mitigations.
Agents can take actions with some autonomy, so unintended actions, called rogue actions, are a growing risk.
invariables: Assurance and governance controls apply to all risks, by all parties, across the whole AI development lifecycle.
Each risk must be mapped to the party that can enact its controls: the model creator, the model consumer, or both.
Data can be poisoned before ingestion, during processing or training, or in storage, so data protection must cover each stage.
principles: Lifecycle view: the security team follows each risk through the whole AI development process, not only the model.
Role mapping: each organization identifies whether it is a model creator, a model consumer, or both, and applies the matching controls.
Data integrity: model creators sanitize training data and control access to models and data.
Self assessment: security teams use the risk self assessment to find which risks apply to them.

papers.title: An Introduction to Google's Approach for Secure AI Agents
papers.source_org: Google
axioms: Agents act as proxies for humans and inherit their privileges to reach resources and take actions.
Underlying models are non-deterministic, so agent behavior is not always repeatable even with the same input.
Higher autonomy increases the scope and impact of errors and the exposure to malicious actors.
The two key agent risks are rogue actions and sensitive data disclosure.
Output rendered without validation can leak data, for example through crafted image URLs in Markdown, and can lead to cross-site scripting.
invariables: Every agent must have a well-defined set of controlling human users.
Systems must reliably tell instructions from an authorized user apart from other input, especially untrusted data.
Agents must be prevented from escalating their own privileges beyond pre-authorized scopes.
Users must be able to inspect and revoke any authority delegated to an agent.
Agent logs must be protected because they hold sensitive data.
principles: Human controllers: the system requires explicit human confirmation before critical or irreversible actions, such as large deletions or security setting changes.
Limited powers: the agent platform aligns permissions with the agent's purpose and current user intent at runtime, beyond static least privilege.
Observable actions: developers log inputs, tools invoked, parameters, outputs, and where feasible reasoning steps, in secure central logging.
Characterized actions: tool owners label each action, for example read-only versus state-changing, so policy engines and reviewers can act on it.
Defense in depth: Google pairs deterministic runtime policy engines outside the model with reasoning-based defenses inside it.
Distinct identities: shared or team agents get distinct identities and clear authorization models to prevent cross-user data access.

papers.title: The Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix
papers.source_org: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
axioms: Agentic AI systems differ from stateless model calls because they act on their own, keep memory, call tools, and connect to outside systems.
Security frameworks built for generative AI do not always extend to agentic AI.
Agency is what a system is allowed to do; autonomy is how far it can act without a human.
The matrix defines four scopes: no agency, prescribed agency, supervised agency, and full agency.
Risk grows as an agent moves from read-only workflows to acting and starting tasks on its own.
invariables: Every action of consequence in a Scope 2 system needs explicit human approval.
Even fully autonomous Scope 4 systems need humans to keep oversight and the ability to step in.
Controls must match the scope, so the organization must first assess which scope each agent use case is in.
principles: Scope first: the organization assesses each agent use case against the four scopes and sets controls for that scope.
Identity by scope: the system owner adds agent authentication, delegated identity, and continuous identity checks as agency grows.
Progressive deployment: the organization builds security capabilities before moving an agent to a higher scope.
Scope governance: the organization sets a review process for moving any agent to a higher scope.
Monitoring by scope: the operator watches agent behavior at a level that matches the scope.

papers.title: Taxonomy of Failure Modes in AI Agents
papers.source_org: Microsoft
papers.date_published: April 24, 2025 (from the URL; not checked on the page)
axioms: Agentic AI systems bring new failure modes and also make some existing AI failure modes worse.
Failure modes fall under two pillars, security and safety, and each can be novel to agents or already known.
Cross-domain prompt injection, where instructions hide in data the agent reads, is described as the most significant failure mode.
Agent memory can be poisoned so that later actions follow an attacker's instructions.
Agents can be compromised, injected, or impersonated within a multi-agent system.
invariables: Each agent needs a unique identity so its actions can be traced and controlled.
Memory must be protected with trust boundaries and the least access needed.
Users must be able to give informed consent before agents take actions for them.
principles: Agent identity: the system owner gives every agent a unique identity.
Memory hardening: the system owner sets trust boundaries and least access on agent memory.
Control flow control: the system owner limits which steps and tools an agent can run.
Environment isolation: the system owner runs agents in isolated environments.
Logging and monitoring: the operator records and watches agent actions.
Injection controls: the system owner treats outside content as untrusted and applies controls for cross-domain prompt injection.

papers.title: Agentic AI Security: Threats, Defenses, Evaluation, and Open Challenges (arXiv 2510.23883)
papers.source_org: Academic survey by Anshuman Chhabra, Shrestha Datta, Shahriar Kabir Nahin, and Prasant Mohapatra (from the arXiv page)
papers.date_published: October 27, 2025 (arXiv v1). The arXiv comment says it was published in IEEE Access.
axioms: Agentic AI with planning, tool use, memory, and autonomy brings security risks that differ from both AI safety and traditional software security.
Agents act across web, software, and physical settings, so attacks can cause real actions.
Defenses fall into user-focused, agent-focused, and system-focused groups, and each has tradeoffs.
Physically embodied agents add risks such as sensor spoofing.
invariables: User-focused defenses depend on human checks, so they do not scale to autonomous agents and fail when the user is the attacker.
Defenses built into the model often need retraining and can fail against adaptive attacks.
Claims about a defense must be tested with benchmarks and adaptive attackers.
principles: Runtime enforcement: the system owner places guardrails outside the model that restrict or adjust agent actions while they run.
Layered guardrails: the system owner combines several defense types instead of relying on one.
Secure by design: agent builders plan security into the agent before deployment.
Rigorous testing: researchers test attacks and defenses with shared benchmarks and metrics.

papers.title: TRiSM for Agentic AI: A Review of Trust, Risk, and Security Management in LLM-based Agentic Multi-Agent Systems (arXiv 2506.04133)
papers.source_org: Academic review by Shaina Raza, Ranjan Sapkota, Manoj Karkee, and Christos Emmanouilidis (from the arXiv page)
axioms: LLM-based agentic multi-agent systems differ from traditional AI agents in how they plan, coordinate, and use tools.
Multi-agent systems add risks such as coordination failures, collusion, and cascading failures between agents.
Prompt injection and memory poisoning are threats specific to agentic systems.
Trust, risk, and security management for these systems can be organized into five pillars: explainability, ModelOps, security, privacy, and lifecycle governance.
invariables: Agent systems in high-stakes fields need governance and audit across their whole lifecycle.
Coordination and tool use must be measured to be managed; the authors propose two metrics for this.
Agent systems need stronger defenses against adversarial attacks and standard benchmarks before they can be trusted in real deployments.
principles: Pillar approach: the governance team manages agent systems across the five TRiSM pillars.
Measure coordination: the evaluation team scores how agents enable each other and how well they use tools.
Protect data: the system owner uses encryption and privacy controls for data that agents handle.
Audit trail: the governance team sets clear audit protocols for agent systems.

papers.title: MLCommons AILuminate Benchmark
papers.source_org: MLCommons
axioms: Generative AI chat systems can produce harmful content across many hazard types.
AILuminate groups hazards into twelve categories: physical, non-physical, and contextual hazards.
Jailbreak attempts lower a system's safety compared with its normal behavior.
Version 1.0 covers single-turn chats only, so hazards that need long or repeated chats, such as bias, are out of scope.
invariables: Tests use a public practice prompt set and a separate private prompt set for the official test.
Grades compare each system's violating responses with a reference system.
Results apply only to the languages tested, which are English and French for now.
principles: Shared taxonomy: benchmark users classify hazards with the AILuminate categories.
Hidden test set: the benchmark owner keeps official prompts private to limit training on the test.
Resilience measure: the jailbreak benchmark measures the drop from normal safety to under-attack safety.
Graded results: the benchmark owner reports overall and per-hazard grades for each system tested.

papers.title: Agentic AI Top 10 Vulnerability (Precize)
papers.source_org: Precize (GitHub project)
axioms: AI agents bring security risks that are not covered by lists built for LLMs alone.
Agents can be hijacked through their authorization and control paths.
Agents that touch critical systems can cause harm well beyond a single response.
Agent memory, context, and knowledge bases can be manipulated or poisoned.
Multi-agent orchestration and agent supply chains open new attack paths.
invariables: Each risk in the list needs a description, examples, and mitigations.
Agent actions have an impact chain, so the blast radius of a compromised agent must be limited.
A human checker must stay in the loop where the risk calls for it.
principles: Authorization control: the system owner limits what an agent may do and checks who controls it.
Blast radius limits: the system owner restricts how far one agent's failure can spread.
Memory protection: the system owner guards agent memory and context against tampering.
Supply chain checks: the system owner verifies agent dependencies and tools.
Time checks: the system owner guards against attacks that use timing or delayed execution.

papers.title: OWASP GenAI Red Teaming Manual Version 1.0
papers.source_org: OWASP GenAI Security Project
papers.date_published: October 20, 2026 (resource page). The PDF cover says October 2026.
axioms: Generative AI systems produce non-deterministic output, so one test run does not show how a model behaves across repeated attempts.
Prompt injection can arrive through any content the model reads, including documents, web pages, tool output, and MCP server responses.
System and developer prompts can be extracted by users, so anything placed in them can leak.
Model files from untrusted sources can carry code that runs when the file is loaded.
Agents that hold tool access can turn one injected instruction into a chain of real actions, such as cascading deletions.
invariables: Red team engagements must run under written authorization with a defined scope and abort conditions.
Testers must use dedicated test accounts and tenant isolation, not real user accounts or production tenants.
Agent testing must run in sandboxes that disconnect production tools and data.
Untrusted data must never enter the model's context with the authority of a system prompt.
Teams must never execute an untrusted model file outside an isolated environment.
Evidence from an engagement must be stored encrypted and handled as sensitive data.
principles: Least privilege: the deploying team grants tools and MCP servers only the API scopes a task needs, during both testing and production.
Enforceable boundaries: the system owner places security controls outside the model, where the model cannot bypass them through its output.
No secrets in prompts: developers never use system or developer prompts as a secret store for keys, credentials, or hidden rules.
Re-validation of tools: operators re-check MCP server and tool definitions after each change, to catch a rug pull where a trusted tool turns malicious.
Controlled engagement: the red team works in phases, with scoping, threat modeling, testing, and reporting, and stops when an abort condition is met.
Evidence handling: testers record prompts, outputs, and tool calls for each finding so that the result can be reproduced and fixed.

papers.title: OWASP LLM Exploit Generation Phase 2: Agentic vs. Classic Offensive Approaches (LLM Exploit Generation Guide 2.0)
papers.source_org: OWASP GenAI Security Project, Threat Intelligence Initiative
papers.date_published: October 27, 2026 (resource page). The PDF cover says Version 1.0, October 2026.
axioms: Hosted frontier models completed all tasks given in this study, while every local DeepSeek variant tested failed to complete a single Cybench task.
On the classic track, a novice reached account takeover largely by cut and paste, because the operator could recognize a guardrail and reframe the request.
Multi-agent frameworks carried out reconnaissance, staging discovery, and exploit research without intervention before provider guardrails stopped them.
The scaffolding around the model, such as tools and prompts, changed results more than the choice of model did.
The first limits the testers hit were operational, such as guardrails, rate limits, and environment errors, rather than model capability.
Nearly every run needed a human with domain knowledge to break a loop, fix an environment error, or run the final step.
invariables: Guardrails in this study delayed both the classic and agentic tracks but stopped neither.
A guardrail that fails under a simple retry or rephrasing only delays a user; it does not prevent the attack.
Local models that answer to no provider have no provider guardrails to stop them.
principles: Retry testing: defenders judge a guardrail by what it does on the second and later attempts, not only on whether it fires once.
Scaffold-aware evaluation: evaluators report the agent scaffolding, tools, and operator help used, because these change outcomes more than the model choice.
Intervention logging: testers record each operator intervention, such as guardrail reframing, tool fixes, loop breaking, and manual completion of a final step.
