Realistic constraints: evaluators measure what AI offers a threat actor under real limits, such as cost ceilings, rate limits, and provider guardrails.

papers.title: OWASP GenAI Data Security Best Practices v2, Part 1
papers.source_org: OWASP GenAI Security Project
papers.date_published: November 3, 2026 (resource page). The PDF cover says Version 2.0, Part 1, October 2026.
axioms: The context window merges content from many trust domains, so any content that reaches the model can influence any output.
Prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, and tool call manipulation remain unsolved at the model layer.
Data in GenAI systems spreads into derived forms such as embeddings, observability traces, and fine-tuned adapter weights.
Static controls lose value as agents, tools, and integrations are added to a system.
The model can leak through memorization, repeat retrieved content, follow injected instructions, and reveal reasoning traces.
invariables: Lifecycle controls such as retention and erasure must reach every derived asset, so a deletion that leaves embeddings, traces, or adapter weights behind is not compliant.
Every GenAI data security program must assume that any content reaching the model can influence any output.
AI data security posture telemetry must reach the SIEM in a normalized format.
Existing incident response playbooks must be extended for GenAI, not duplicated.
Owner assignments for AI data security must be explicit and reviewed each quarter.
principles: Data minimization: builders send the model only the data a task needs and the user may access, using retrieval limits, payload schemas, and per-call scoping.
Isolation and least privilege: operators enforce per-tenant, per-user, per-session, and per-agent boundaries in vector indexes, memory, tool credentials, and agent identities.
Human approval: the system requires a human checkpoint before an agent takes an irreversible or high-impact action.
Integrity and provenance: data owners sign artifacts and keep attestations and dataset bills of materials, and reject tampered data at each ingestion step.
Continuous posture management: security teams run ongoing discovery, classification, access review, and DLP across the GenAI data surface.
Zero trust in the model: architects treat no model output as trusted and no system prompt rule as enforced, and add output filtering, schema checks, tool sandboxing, and human approval.

papers.title: Design Tenets for Agent Identity Management Systems
papers.source_org: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Cybersecurity Insights blog
axioms: Large language models accept data and instructions as a single stream of tokens, so data and control are not separated.
An agent with standing or broad privileges can be hijacked to reach sensitive data or carry out high-impact transactions.
Static or long-lived bearer tokens let attackers who steal them keep persistent, unauthorized access.
If an agent's activity cannot be linked to the person or entity that started it, high-impact actions cannot be attributed to a responsible party.
Agents act at a scale and speed that humans and most deterministic automation cannot match.
Current standards and technology do not yet meet all ten tenets.
invariables: Separation between an agent's reasoning and its permissions must be enforced by architecture, since the model does not provide it.
Activity logs that the agent itself can reach or change cannot serve as reliable evidence.
Several tenets are often needed together to mitigate one attack, such as a confused deputy attack.
principles: Distinct agent identification: agentic infrastructure gives each agent a unique, cryptographically verifiable identity, separate from human users and service accounts.
Linking, delegation, and attenuation: systems cryptographically link each agent to the entity that tasked it through the whole execution, and narrow delegated rights.
Least and zero standing privilege: agents hold no rights when idle and get only the minimum scope a task needs, under separation of duties.
Short-lived authorization: access grants are just in time, time bound, and audience specific, and each tool call is checked at runtime and can be revoked.
Mandates and constraints: the task originator signs a mandate that states the intended outcome and limits for the agent's actions.
Deterministic access decisions: organizations use deterministic decisions as the main access control, with probabilistic signals only as input.
Human-in-the-loop triggers: each organization sets risk thresholds that route agent actions to the right human authority for review.
Immutable evidence: the enterprise keeps an append-only, tamper-evident record of agent identity, delegated intent, and actions, separate from the agent.

papers.title: Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation
papers.source_org: CISA, with NIST CAISSI and NSA SISC (as listed in the document)
papers.date_published: October 16, 2026 (CISA resource page). The PDF says October 2026, Version 1.0, PP-26-4396, TLP:CLEAR.
axioms: An SI control incident occurs when an agent takes significant uninstructed actions that break operator policies, controls, or human oversight.
Actions caused by prompt injection or a backdoored model count as instructed actions, not as the primary cause of an SI control incident.
An SI control incident can cause a cybersecurity incident, but it can also involve actions outside cyber domains, such as unauthorized financial transactions.
SI agents are nondeterministic and can act on their own, which adds concerns beyond standard incident response practice.
Monitors that use SI models to oversee SI agents may add their own weaknesses.
invariables: Agents must not be able to access or interfere with the monitoring processes and logs that watch them.
Monitored model output must be treated as possibly containing exploits aimed at the monitors.
Training, evaluation, or deployment should start or resume only when senior leadership accepts the assessed risk.
Security controls must be built on the expectation that agents will often find and exploit misconfigurations and vulnerabilities.
principles: Least privilege: organizations limit each SI agent's access to sensitive data, systems, and tools to what its task needs.
Network allowlisting: operators limit agent network access with a strict allowlist and route required access through a monitored gateway.
Kill switch: organizations build ways to quickly block, contain, or stop agent activity when an incident or near miss is detected.
Layered monitoring: operators watch the model, its agent scaffolding, the host, and the network, and cross-check with models from different families.
Tamper-resistant evidence: organizations keep logs with reliable timestamps that rebuild agent trajectories, tool calls, reasoning traces, and control decisions.
Shutdown policy: organizations define shutdown rules for control failures and monitor outages, and shut down affected agent runs on detection.
Verified recovery: teams revoke exposed credentials, rebuild affected environments, and verify containment before agents resume.
